On the Orders of the Day:

As relating to a matter of very considerable interest at the present time, 1 would like to ask if the Government has any information to give to the House and the country on the prevailing famine in India.
Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council):	Mr. Speaker, a
committee of public spirited citizens in Toronto some time ago organized for the purpose of collecting relief for the sufferers from the famine in India and at their request the Government communicated,

through the Imperial authorities, with the Government of India tendering this relief and inquiring whether relief in grain or cash would be the more acceptable. Two communications have been received in reference to the matter. One is that the Government of India gratefully accept the offer of the 'Committee and express a wish for cash rather 'than grain. Another statement has followed. After stating that the attention of the Government of India has been drawn to certain statements which appeared in the Canadian press to the effect that millions of British subjects are starving, they point out that the statement is not . correct and they send the following statement which they ask to have made public:
" Food position in India though undoubtedly grave has no resemblance to descriptions in Toronto circular which is exaggerated and in many parts untrue. Owing to failure of autumn rains, to serious epidemic of influenza which attacked two-thirds of the population, and accounted for -six million deaths, and to absence of large number of young men on military service, area sown with winter crops very short. This, in conjunction with general rise in wages and in standard of living, with inflated currency and reflex action of world prices, has caused foodstuffs to rise to unprecedented prices causing hardship to many sections of the population. But resisting power of people is greater than ever before and although prices are double those of famine year of 1900 number of relief in April was only 337,000 against five and a quarter million in April 1900. Plague is less virulent than usual and no report ejther from private or official sources of any deaths' from starvation have been received. Though there have been food riots in some places they are not as stated in circular of daily occurrence. Thanks to excellent monsoon in 1917 walls in most parts are still holding water, mails are delivered regularly and business is brisk. Stocks of food grains are low but special measures have been taken to conserve supplies and wheat has been imported from Australia. Given normal monsoon there should be enough food until autumn crops are in sight. At the same time low stocks and excessive prices have created situation which is causing great anxiety to Government of India and serious hardship is undoubtedly being experienced by many sections of population." End.
The 'Secretary of State for India adds that season such as now being experienced in India inevitably occasions suffering and privation to poorer and more helpless classes and gives ample scope for private charity in addition to Stat^ relief.
Who is the author of this essay?

That is a cable from Lord Milner sent at the request of the Secretary of State for India to be made public here in Canada.

On motion that the House go into Committee on Bill No. 19 to consolidate and amend the Railway Act:
Will the minister explain the necessity of an amending Bill?

The Bill that we are going into Committee on is the consolidation of the Railway Act. We did pass a Bill to amend the old Railway Act which now stands for third reading. If this Bill goes through its third reading, I intend to withdraw the other Bill.

Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to a letter I have received from Winnipeg under date of April 11, 1919, referring to a matter that came before the Special Committee that dealt with this particular Bill. The letter is as follows:
Enclosed please find a clipping from to-day's Manitoba Free Press, which states that Locomotive engineers in some instances deliberately kill cattle on the railroad tracks1. I, for one, repudiate such a statement, and these people should be brought to time land made to prove their case. Such a statement should not be allowed to go unchallenged, and I trust that as you are an ex-railway employee in engine service, and know the danger of such an undertaking, you will see your way clear to have this matter remedied. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I have very
grave doubts as to whether the hon. gentleman is in order in raising a discussion upon the mere motion, that I do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee on a Bill. The hon. gentleman would be in order in bringing this matter up in Committee.

Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Short title.

Mr. Chairman, it will be remembered that this Bill has been before the House of Commons and the Senate during the last two or three sessions. A special committee .of this House took evidence from a great many persons interested in the different sections. This Bill contains altogether 461 sections, and with the exception of 35 sections no changes have be^n made in the original Bill as passed by this House and the Senate. I thought we might take up these sections in which no change has been made either by the House or the Senate, and after passing those come back to the 35 sections which have been amended,- some in the Senate and some in the House. If that suggestion meets with the approval of the Committee perhaps we can make faster progress than by taking up the Bill clause by clause. Of course, if we come to any clause on which any hon. member wishes to take issue we could take it up and dispose of! it.
Would the hon. minister give us the clauses which were amended?
I have a list of 'the clauses in which no changes have been made, and also a list of those in which changes have been made.
Will the minister give us the list of clauses in which changes were made?

Is there no change
in 374?
No.
It has been changed since the original Act was passed.

Oh, yes. There are two clauses that the member for East Lambton (Mr. J. E. Armstrong) wishes to discuss. Then, of course, there is the power clause, with reference to the dispute in Toronto. Nearly all the others are clauses to which, I think, no objection will be taken.

Which are the two
clauses that the member for East Lambton wishes to deal with?
3 and 258. They are with reference to placing Canadian steamships under the Board of Railway Commissioners
Are they still in the Bill?
The special committee passed them without any change. Clauses that any member wishes to take objection to, we could allow to stand and discuss with the 35 clauses to which amendments have been made.

I suggest that the minister put on Hansard the amendments that were proposed, but defeated; also the clauses to which amendments were proposed, such as the power clause, and sections 34 and 258, that the member for East Lambton refers to. These are contentious clauses, although they have not been amended. We do not want to have it understood that only these 35 clauses which have been amended are contentious. Let us put in one class all the clauses that were amended and all that are contentious or in respect of which proposed amendments were defeated; then we can go ahead with the rest.

I have not before me the amendments that were proposed in the special committee, but I have had printed all x the amendments made in the special committee. I have three copies here; the others will be here in fifteen or twenty minutes, and a copy will be supplied to each member. If, in considering the non-contentious clauses, we come to a clause which any member wishes to discuss, we can let it stand and deal with it when we come to consider the sections to which amendments have been made or which any members

wish to discuss. I think that the whole discussion will come down to four or five important matters. There is the Toronto matter, the telephone question, the matter of railway crossings-there, are not more than four or five altogether. So that if the Committee will pass the clauses to which there are no objection we shall save time.

It is quite proper that we should take up first and get through with these non-contentious clauses. What has become of this contention between the Niagara Power Company and the city of Toronto? I could never understand why it was imported into the general Railway Act. However, it is in the Railway Bill, and I should like to know how the matter stands.

When this Bill was before the House three years ago the House adopted a clause with reference to that matter. When the Bill went to the Senate the Senate' amended that clause, and they amended it again last year. Last year's clause was put in by the Senate this year. It is section 374, which reads in part:-
Any specific powers inconsistent with the provisions of this section and conferred on any company by any special or other Act or authority of the Parliament of Canada or of any province shall not be affected by the provisions of this section, but if any municipality complains to the Board that any company whether incorporated by special or other Act or authority of the Parliament of Canada is exercising: its powers oppressively or in bad faith the Board may hear such complaint and if it sees fit supervise the exercise of such powers : Provided always that whenever any company incorporated by Special Act of the Parliament of Canada acquires the assets of a company operating within a municipality, which said municipality has the right by agreement to purchase any of the assets of such company, then and in every such case the municipality may enforce its rights under such agreement as fully as if such purchase had not been made and may enforce against such purchaser the provisions of such agreement as if it were the original party entering into such agreement with the municipality.
That is the way it came from the Senate, and the special committee passed it as it came from the Senate. Although this clause is in the list of those to which there are no amendments, still, when we come to it, it is for the Committee to say whether they -will accept the Senate amendment as passed by the special committee, or whether they will further amend the clause.

I know I have no right to go to the middle of the Bill to ask about this clause, but I want the Committee to have some general idea as to how the matter stands between the two contending

forces. Can the minister tell me whether they have reached any conclusion?

The matter stands exactly as before. The Toronto city authorities were not satisfied with the clause as it now stands in the Bill, and I do not know that the others were very well satisfied either.. This is a kind of settlement that the Senate thought might probably be fair to both parties, but it is now for the Committee to say Whether they will concur with the Senate or amend the clause further.
We certainly have nothing to do with settling the dispute. We are creating legislation under which the parties can negotiate. That is about as far as we can go.
That is the situation exactly.

Section agreed to.

On section 2-definitions:

We now return to the clauses that were allowed to stand. Some of them are not contentious. In paragraph (b), .subsection 4 of section 2, strike out the word " minister " and substitute therefor the word " Board." Under the Railway Act, returns were heretofore sent to tire minister; now they are to be sent to the Board of Railway Commissioners.

Why are they not
sent direct to the Dominion Statistician?

They are sent to the
Dominion Statistician as well.

No, these are the regular railway statistics. 'Sections 380 and 381 are amended so that the statistics are sent to the Dominion Statistician and to the Board of Railway Commissioners. The former will publish them; the latter will have them for their own information.

With reference to subsection 14, I may say that in Alberta a justice of the peace has jurisdiction over the whole province, but this subsection as drafted limits the jurisdiction of a justice of the peace to the " district, county, riding, division." I should like, therefore, to have the word " province " inserted before, the word " district " in the second line of subsection 14.
Why not say " justice " means a justice of the peace, and stop there? The jurisdiction is defined by the local legislature.
What I want to avoid is that there shall be no dispute as to the jurisdiction of our justices of the peace if they take cognizance of the matters mentioned in section 2.
That would not be satisfactory to Ontario, because our justices of the peace are appointed for the county, not for the province.

The jurisdiction of a justice of the peace is defined by the statute. It must be so defined in Ontario.
Mr. .BOYS:	Only for the county.

Then when you come before a justice of the peace who has not jurisdiction under Dominion statute, you can simply raise the question of his jurisdiction. But I think the word " justice " should be defined as follows:	"Justice"
means " Justice of the Peace." That is sufficient.
The clause as it stands in the Bill is the same as it has been in the previous Acts for a number of years. This is an exact copy.
That is no reason why we should not amend it now.

If the word "province" is inserted before the word " district," that would cover the whole case.
Amendment (Mr. H. A. Mackie) agreed to.

I omitted to refer to subsection 13. This should be amended so that when a judge is authorized to do any act or make any order, he shall be deemed to act not as persona non designata, but he shall have all the power of the court, acting for the court, especially in directing other persons to be notified, or in making amendments, or in regard to expropriations where it appears that there are separate and distinct interests, and where one sum is offered for compensation for the whole land, and the company should make separate offers to each, so that if one person accepts, he may get out of the proceedings and not be compelled to have his interest diminished by reason of the cost of arbitration, which cost he cannot, under the circumstances, avoid. If the Committee will permit me to refer to clause 215, it will be seen that under that clause application may be made to the court or to a judge for directions. For instance, paragraph (c) reads:
A notification that within ten days after the service of this notice, or, where the notice is served by publication, within one month after the first publication thereof, the party to whom the notice is addressed does not give notice to the company that he accepts the sum offered by the company, either he or the company will be entitled to apply to have the compensation fixed 1919Tbitrati0n aS provided in the Railway Act,
In the definitions, an owner is the person who is capable of granting title, but it is quite possible for a person to have an interest in land under agreement of sale, which, in the western provinces, is similar to a promise for sale in Quebec, and not to be able to give title. At the same time, he has an interest in the land, and it might be possible for him to accept the amount offered to him separately, if a separate amount were mentioned for him. Under present circumstances, he is not able to do that, and if any other person who is interested in the land desires to create a great deal of costs or trouble, the person who would be willing to withdraw by accepting a certain sum of money is compelled to stand the cost of an arbitration and possibly the cost of an appeal. In the case of a judge as defined, should there be an appeal, this circumstance arises:	If one
of the parties is dissatisfied and gives notice of appeal, the first thing that is discussed is that the judge is persona non designata, and there is no appeal from his order or direction or judgment, and if the party wishes to take any appeal at all. he will have to wait until there is an arbitration, but if there is no arbitration and one party desires to take any advantage of an 
appeal, then he is prevented from taking an appeal by reason of the fact that the ' judge is designated as a person to arbitrate and not as a judge of the court. What I am asking for in subsection 13 is that the judge shall be designated as a judge of the court, and that his decisions, orders and directions shall have the force of a judgment and. not simply the force of a direction coming from a person who stands in the position of a person designated.
That might be better put as an amendment to another clause.
In clause 232, there is an appeal from the award. Would not that cover the point?

If clause 232 contains the amendment I desire to suggest to the Committee,- some difficulty mFght arise about turning .back to the definition of the word " judge ", because the definition of the word " judge " would rule in clause 232. I am afraid the amendment must be made in clause 2, subclause 13, so as to give the judge the power of the court, and it would -have to be repeated in clause 232.	.

I would ask my hon. friend (Mr. H. A. Mackie) whether he is quite sure that the laws of his province do not follow those of the older provinces which have Acts called " Judges Orders Enforcement Acts," which put any duty of a judge outside of court statutes in the same position as if he were acting wholly as a judge. We have that in Ontario, and, I imagine, also in the other older provinces.

Would the minister
kindly postpone the consideration of this Bill until every member has a copy of the amendments sent by the special committee to the House of Commons Committee? Some of the members have not had an opportunity of considering them.

The hon. member was present on' the Committee and knows the amendments that were proposed, and I hardly think it is fair that we should postpone proceeding with the Bill. We know what the amendments are when they are mentioned here.

I would suggest that it might be well to postpone the consideration of any long amendments, but there is no need to do that in the case of small, simple amendments such as changing a word or tvvo.

Mr. H. A. iMAlOKI'E: In answer to the inquiry of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat), the following cases have been decided on the point on which I touched regarding the question whether a judge is persona non designata or has the power of the court:-	j
Marsan vs. G.T.P- (2 Alta. Law Reports): Saunders vs. E. D. & B. (6 Alta. Law Reports) : Gauthier vs. C.N.R. (7 Alta. Law Reports). In every one of those cases the question was discussed whether an order given by a judge sitting as an arbitrator had the force and effect of a judgment of a court. If it has not, you may not appeal from it; if it has, you may appeal. A very peculiar situation has arisen, in this way: Where notice has been given of an interim direction by a judge, and notice of appeal has been taken from that direction, subsequently, if an arbitration was held, you could not appeal from the arbitration because, it would be contended, you had appealed from the direction. Then the question would be; should we have appealed from the direction? This question has arisen, and I should like to have the point cleared up.	'

The doctrine which the hon. member expounds is well known to the law. I did not have the opportunity of attending the Committee when this Bill was being considered. The question is, was it the intention of the Committee that the judge should sit as a judge and discharge the ordinary functions of a judge, from whose direction there would be an appeal? If it was the intention of the ' Committee that the judge's decision should be final, there is no necessity for providing for an appeal. If- that was not the intention, we should make it clear what was intended.

I think there is no question that it was the intention of the Committee that there should be an appeal, because the Committee dealt with section 232 in which an appeal is provided for. I do not think the point raised by the hon. member for Edmonton applies in so far as the province of Ontario is concerned, unless it be on a question of practice. If his idea is that we should expand the meaning of the word judge so that any action on the part of a judge acting under this Act should be subject to the ordinary appeals and consolidated rules of the province of Ontario, that would necessitate a complete revision of the rules and would revolutionize our practice. Section 232 lays down that an appeal shall lie, and the proceedings that are to be taken. It was the intention of the Committee that that appeal should be open either to the railway company or to the person whose land was being expropriated.
If the sections make it clear what the intention of the Committee was, I think we should be satisfied.

I do-not think there can be any doubt as to the intention of the Committee, because section 232 in plain English provides for an appeal. All that paragraph (13) of section 2 does is to say that a "judge" means a judge of a superior or county court, and I think that definition is necessary, otherwise it might be held that "judge" meant only a judge of a superior court. When we say that it means a judge of a superior or county court we realize that the appeal provided for under section 232 would lie from either.

Section 232 says: "Within one month after receiving from the arbitrator .... a written notice of the making of the award." It is quite clear that the appeal is from the award. My hon. friend from South Simcoe has stated my position correctly. I desire to revolutionize this section so that an arbitration judge shall be constituted a judge of a court from whose judgments there shall be an appeal, just as in the case of a judge of a court.

I rather agree with my hon. friend from South Simcoe. I would point out to my hon. friend (Mr. H. A. Mackie) that section 232 provides for dealing directly with questions of fact upon the evidence taken before an arbitrator. Further, paragraph (7) of section 2 defines a "court" as follows:
" Court " means a superior court of the province or district, and wihen used with respect to any proceedings for the ascertainment or payment, either to the person entitled, or into court,
of compensation	includes the county
court of the county where the lands lie; and "'county court " and " superior oourt " are to be interpreted according to the Interpretation Act and Amendments thereto.
So we have all the machinery possible under section 232 to cover anything a judge may do as arbitrator.

I quite realize that there is an appeal from every act of a judge of a court as designated here, but if he is sitting as an arbitrator in an arbitration he has not the power of a judge of a court, but of an arbitrator; he is in the position of a person designated. If there is no arbitration there is no appeal

of an intermediate character up to the point of arbitration, because one cannot	appeal	unless there is an
award.	Section 232 is the only one
under which an appeal is provided for. Suppose under section 215 you go to a judge designated as arbitrator and ask him to direct that John Smith or Peter Jones be summoned before a certain board for the settlement of differences and some one desires to take an appeal from that. There can only be an appeal from the award. The judge should be a judge of the court and not an arbitrator purely and simply, and all he does should have the force and effect of a judgment from which we may appeal, whether there is an award or not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. member state his amendment?
It would take me some time to formulate it. I did not expect that the Bill would be taken up this afternoon, nor that it would be dealt with ir. this way.
Where is the authority in this Act to go before a judge to have an order to compel somebody else to appear before a board?

Section 215 says:
(c) A notification that if within ten days after the service of this notice, or, where the notice is served by publication, within one month after the first publication thereof, the party to whom the notice is .addressed does not give notice to the company that he accepts the sum offered by the company, either he or the company will be entitled to apply to have the compensation fixed by arbitration as provided in the Railway Act, 1919.
A notice to this effect must be served upon the opposite party preliminary to proceeding to arbitration to fix compensation' or damages. If an application is made under this section, it is not to a judge of the court, but to a judge appointed as arbitrator.

If the party to whom you serve notice is in default and does not accept within ten days you just set your case for trial. That is the law of Quebec. If the other party does not appear it is an ex paTte arbitration. You do not need to have an order from the court 5 p.m. to set your case. You set it de jure. After you set your case a man is debarred from pleading further unless he receives permission.
Mr, H. A. MACKIE: My point is that it is before a man acting as an arbitrator and not as a judge.

He has all the powers of an arbitrator, and you proceed the same as . if you had three arbitrators under the old system. If a man is in default you do the same as in an ordinary process-we call it "inscription" in our province-for trial, and the otl|er party may appear to crossexamine witnesses. In our province that would be allowed even though he had not disputed or filed an appearance. He may appear in person at the time of the trial, and has a right to cross-examine witnesses , if he desires, but he is barred from filing pleadings. When a man declines to accept your amount and says he wants so much for his land, that is a complete answer to your notice-I am not sure what it is designated in Ontario, whether it is "bill of particulars." If he does not answer he is in default and you inscribe the case before the court and proceed.

Suppose a railway company offers a lump sum for a piece of land in which four or five parties are interested. One man may ask a certain sum for his interest, and it may not be accepted, with the result that there is an . arbitration. The company or some individual interested in the land appeals, and A or B, who is willing to accept a certain sum and avoid further .proceedings, has no remedy. He has no judgment in his favour. Any direction that the court gives is a direction from an arbitrator and not a judge and the man must stand the proportion of costs of all proceedings.
No.

That is a question for the final division of the money. When there are several persons interested in the land the money must be paid into court and there must be some machinery to divide the money according to their interest, and the man who took the appeal would have to take the responsibility of costs.
If I were permitted I could get the reports, which I have not with me, and could, convince the Committee that I am absolutely right in my point.

If a man does not dispute a case they cannot charge costs against him. It is a case oi, "II s'en rapporte A justice." If a man wants to dispute it let him bear the costs that are incurred against him.
Mr. BOY'S: 'Sedtion 217 refers only to an absent party, or substitutional service. We de not want an appeal from a judge in regard

to substitutional service. That would only make the costs of arbitration so much more expensive to the parties interested. When a sum is offered by a company and is refused you proceed to arbitration under section 232, and have the right of appeal and unless we want to give further appeals the section is all right as it is. If what my hon. friend is suggesting should become law it would simply mean that when a county judge makes an award . you can appeal from him to the Superior Court in the province and then to the Supreme Court, and from there to the Privy Council. We want to avoid that sort of thing and there is a remedy provided now.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-to what persons, companies and railways applicable:

I move that the section be amended so as to read:
This Act shall, subject as herein provided, apply to all persons, railway companies and railways within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, whether heretofore or hereafter and howsoever incorporated or authorized, except Government railways, to which, however, it shall apply to such extent as is specified in any Act referring or relating thereto.

Why not mention the
Canadian National Railway Act? That is the only Act that is going to regulate the railways. There is only one Act now, as I understand it, that will apply to the Canadian National Railways, the Act passed the other day. The Canadian National Railways include the Intercolonial Railway. I understand the intention is to simplify the system and have as far as possible one uniform law applicable to all. There are only two systems the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific.
There is the Canadian Railways Provident Fund, and we might have some other railways.

The provident fund would not have anything to do with the administration of the railways.
iMr. J. D. REID: We have some railways that have not been transferred to the Canadian National Railways.

Well, others that have
not been transferred come under this Act.
Mr. |J. D. REID: There are railways owned by the Government, but not transferred to the Canadian National Railways.
Owned by the Government but not transferred?
They may not yet have been transferred.
Are there any railways that have not been transferred yet? I cannot understand how the Government can own anything and have the property of it in strangers.

If in a year or two hence a further Act was passed this provision would be necessary. You want it to apply not only to the present but to the future, five or ten years hence. As it is worded now it would apply, but restricted in the manner suggested by the hon. member it would not.

I think it would be better to leave it as it is. We have to consider every Act as standing on its own legs, and this could not refer to an Act that has not been assented to by the Governor General or become law.

This Bill has not been assented to yet but we take it for granted that it will be law as soon as it passes the House. The Government either owns or does not own railways. If it owns railways there is only to be one law regarding their operation. The moment a railway is the property of the Government it comes under the control of the Canadian National Railways; until then it is Tegulated by the general Act.
My friend is asking that this well expressed language "except Government railways" be altered to apply only to the Canadian Government Railway Act.
What I suggest is "except as provided by the Canadian National Railways Act."
I think we should leave this language "except Government railways." Every one understands what it means. What is the use of imparting doubt or surmise into an Act which every one wants to be clear.
We would like to know what the other Acts are. I hate to travel all over the statutes from Confederation to find out what they are.
Exoept where inconsistent with the provisions of the National Railway Act.
That is not what it says.

My hon. friend did not understand me. If he looks at the provisions of the National Railway Act he will find a clause which makes the Railway Act applicable except where inconsistent with the provisions of the National Railway Act.
Yes, hut there is the general Railway Act of Canada, the Canadian National Railway Act and the Intercolonial Railway Act-three of them.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-application to:

There is an additional subsection that it is proposed to insert here. When the Bill was before the House three years ago there was a subsection (c) added reading as follows:
(c) every railway or portion thereof, whether constructed under the authority of the Parliament of Canada or not, now or hereafter owned, controlled, leased or operated by a company wholly or partly within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, or by a company operating a railway wholly or partly within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, whether such ownership, control or first-mentioned operation is acquired or exercised by purchase, lease, agreement or other means whatsoever, and whether acquired or exercised under authority of the Parliament of Canada, or of the legislature of any province, or otherwise howsoever; and every railway or portion thereof, now or hereafter so owned, controlled, leased or operated shall be deemed and is hereby declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. S-9 E. VII, c. 32, s. 11. Am.
That subsection was put into the Bill in this House, but when it went to the Senate they struck it out. The special committee inserted it again. The reason it was put in was to cover a case in the province of Quebec where the Quebec Central railway, incorporated under the Provincial Government and, of course, under the jurisdiction of the Provincial Government, was leased for ninety-nine years by the Canadian Pacific. The result is that a portion of that railway, in so far as operation is concerned, is under the jurisdiction of the Provincial Government while it is really part and parcel of the Canadian Pacific Railway system. This clause is for the purpose of bringing this railway, which is practically owned by the Canadian Pacific, under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. The representatives of the employees in Ottawa were very strong for having this inserted for the protection of the employees, There is also the other question of placing the freight rates under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commissioners.

I do not know that the amendment has been distributed or seen by the members. The object of the amendment is all right, but it may be necessary to consider the wording. The intent of the law, as we understand it in discussing it in Parliament, may not be carried out when we come to analyze the words used. There must be some objection to this subsection if the Senate refused to insert it a couple of years ago. What reasons were adduced for its rejection I do not know.

The Senate said that Parliament's right constitutionally to declare in this general way that every railway should be deemed a railway for the general advantage of Canada was questionable. It said, further, that the question of the invasion of provincial rights bore also upon it and that it was always open tc^ a company to apply to Parliament to have its undertaking declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. It seems to me that the clause which passed this House in 1917, and which has been read oy the minister, expresses in apt words what is desired chiefly by the employees of the railway. Here is a provincial railway operated by the Canadian Pacific; the men get accustomed to the regulations of the Canadian Pacific right along and suddenly they are switched before they know it to a provincial railway, where the regulations may be different as to hand rails, height of bridges and all those things that serve for the protection of the men. They do not desire that there should be this difference between the two railways. They desire that the provincial railway, which to all intents and purposes is the Canadian Pacific, be left under the direction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. I do not think there is any reason why we should not re-enact what this House did in 1917. We should put it up to the Senate that they have not considered it from the aspect I have now given, that the operating rules should be uniform to insure the safety of the men.
I do not want to be understood as objecting, but an amendment of that length ought to be submitted to the members instead of being merely shoved under our noses.
The hon. member was in the House three years ago when we discussed the. clause thoroughly, and I did not think there would be any objection from him.

I am not referring to this clause alone; I understand certain amend-

merits have been adopted by the special committee and will foe submitted to this Committee. I claim that we have not had an opportunity, not being members of the special committee, to study those clauses, I do not object to this clause going through, although I do not believe the safety of the men is any better guarded than under the Quebec Railway Act. Whether this clause is based on the Quebec Act, or the latter is based on this, I do not know, but they are alike.
The employees on the Canadian Pacific railway have uniform rules in connection with the operation of the whole system.
I understand that. I do not object to it.
The representatives of the employees state that the rules are different on this particular line.
That may be, but they have a remedy under the local law the same as they have under the Federal law.
In 1917 we also wanted to put them under the Railway Board as far as rates were concerned.
I am only saying that we ought to have a copy of these amendments before being asked to pass upon them.

The representatives of all the railway brotherhoods urgently requested that this amendment should be included in the Bill. They called attention to the fact that the Quebec Central Railway is not under the control of the Railway Commission, and they were most anxious that the employees who are operating that road should be placed in the same position as other railway employees in Canada.
That does not answer my request to have a chance to look at these amendments before they go through. I have absolute .confidence in the Special Committee, but my name is Thomas-I would like to see.
Does the hon. member want to see the amendment?
Yes, I would like to have time to read it quietly.
I will hand the amendment to the hon. member.

Does this mean that
we are putting .an exclusively provincial road under the control of the Board of
Railway Commissioners? Take, for instance, the railroad between Sydney and Louisburg, which was built by the Dominion Iron and Steel Company under their charter from the local legislature. They are operating the line to some extent as a passenger railway, but largely as a traffic road. Do we put that road under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners?

The railway the hon. gentleman has referred to would not come under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, unless, say, the Canadian Pacific railway purchased 'it and had it declared as a work for the general advantage of Canada. This, clause would not interfere with it so long as the line was not made part and parcel of a through road. The reason for this clause is that judicial doubts were expressed as to whether the Board of Railway Commissioners had jurisdiction in, such a case. If we pass this clause it gives the Board of Railway Commissioners jurisdiction after the road has been purchased or leased-
Or operated.

-or comes under the control or operation of a -through line system. Then the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners extends to it in so far as that board has jurisdiction over the main line.

This amendment provides that if a provincial road is leased, purchased cr owned-I have no objection to ownership -by a company which is partly or wholly under Federal jurisdiction, that road comes under such .jurisdiction. But at the expiration of the lease it remains under Federal jurisdiction, which is what I abject to. Why not add: "Shall be under Federal jurisdiction while such lease or agreement continues?" It seems to me that .would be better. Take the St. Maurice railway between Shawinigan Falls and Three Rivers. Suppose it were leased by the Canadian Pacific Railway, although incorporated by the local legislature, that road would remain under Federal jurisdiction after the lease expired and the Canadian -Pacific surrendered control.
It has to be declared a railway for the general advantage of Canada, and* is brought under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners when transferred either by purchase or lease.
By purchase is all right.

Where railways are
being operated as part of a through system or in conjunction with each other, it is better anyway that they should be under one jurisdiction. While there might he something said for letting the road go back to provincial jurisdiction at the termination of the working agreement or lease, I do not think it is in the interest of the road or of the employees; therefore I would prefer leaving the amendment as it is.

I remember trying to obtain incorporation of a railway exclusively within a certain province, but the Government said: "No, we do not want to incorporate a road like this." If a road is incorporated by the legislature, I admit that for the purpose of better operation it is all right to place it under Federal control while it is operated as part and parcel of another system which is under Federal control. But when the lease has expired why should you force the owners of that line to remain in that position? Why should they not return to the original jurisdiction under which they were incorporated?

As far as this case is concerned, it would not make any difference, for the reason that it is a nine hundred and ninety-nine year lease. But at the same time, is it not almost certain that when a lease is taken of a road it is taken for a long term? You very seldom hear of a lease of a railway for only a few years.
But you are legislating for all railways.
I admit that.

If this is going to be
legislation for the Quebec Central, tet us so state. If it is going to be for all railways, we should not force any railway which may be leased for a term to a larger system to remain under Federal jurisdiction after the lease expires or when the reason for its having been taken under Federal jurisdiction ceases to exist.

Suppose you lived on a
short line which could not get along unless it had connection with a through line; and suppose the short line charged you more for carrying freight ten miles than the through line, under the jurisdiction of the Railway Board, charged for a thousand miles-what would you say then? .

I would go before the
Railway Board and have the rates cut down. I do not think we are so wise that we ought to legislate for these people who
INTr. Bureau.]
have organized companies and put up their money, and tell them that they are making a mistake; and that if they connect for a certain length of time with another line that has a Federal charter, they must stay there forever. I do not believe in that. After the expiration of their agreement with the larger line, they should be enabled to revert to the conditions which existed before they entered into the agreement.
Mr. MlORPHY: The hon. member is overlooking something that will rather upset his argument when it occurs to his mind. The men who work on the main line railways are anxious that any subsidiary lines that are taken over shall have the same appliances, equipment and safety devices and the same general regulations for the safety of the operatives that exist on the large trunk lines. I am informed that many accidents have been brought about by lack of uniformity as between the smaller line and the larger one in the matter of the equipment of brakes and other connecting devices. If at the end of, say, a ten-year lease a local road ceases to be subject to the regulations of the Railway Board and may put on such local equipment and devices as it thinks fit, we shall be right up against the trouble that this section is intended to obviate, namely, lack of uniformity of devices, contrivances and apparatus for the safety of the operatives of the road. If for no other reason than that, I should say that once under the Railway Board, a system should always remain there.

I assume that the Provincial Legislature are just as wise as we are, and that they are able to make laws and regulations for the safety of their citizens just as well as the Federal Government is. If a provincially incorporated company chooses to make an agreement with a larger company which is under Federal jurisdiction, it is right that during the life of the agreement it should be under Federal supervision in such matters as these. But why should we prevent men from following their own inclination and their own wishes in the matter after the agreement has expired? If the only safety exists in the Railway Board or in Federal legislation, then away with the right of the provinces to enact railway legislation-that is What the argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Morphy) comes down to.

There is quite a difference between a local road with limited jurisdiction and a Dominion or Federal

road with an overshadowing jurisdiction. The local road cannot compel uniformity as regards the Dominion road; consequently there should he some paramount power to enforce uniformity of appliances. A local Government may be the best Government in the world for the railway operatives, but it has no power over Federal roads. While the local Government might be as advanced in the matter of railway legislation as the Federal Government, still, it might choose different kinds of appliances from those used on the Federal road, and it would be like the tail wagging the dog; the smaller road would attempt to set up its standards of uniformity against the equally good but different standards of the main line. 'My idea is that uniformity is the crux of the situation and that some - paramount power ought to rest in the Dominion through the medium of the Railway' Commission.

The point made by my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) is very clear to me. I assume that there is no intention on the part of this legislation to interfere in any way with provincial jurisdiction over provincial railways. If a privately-owned road passes over to the Canadian Pacific Railway, for instance, there is no objection to its being under the jurisdiction of the Board while it is held by the Canadian Pacific. But the member for Three Rivers contends that when the lease terminates, we should not prevent the company from going back to its former status if it wishes to do so. We should so construct our legislation that when the instrument which creates the jurisdiction terminates, the locally owned company may go back to its former jurisdiction.

The point raised by the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) is of paramount importance to railway employees throughout the country so far as it relates to safety appliances. Notwithstanding anything that may be said as to the efficiency of any megsure that a Provincial Legislature may enact with regard to safety appliances, you cannot have uniformity where nine provinces are dealing with the same thing. It is essential that there be uniformity in appliances on freight and passenger cars, and in respect of equipment of all kinds. Let me illustrate by referring to one of the appliances in connection with freight equipment on railways in Canada and the United States that come under the jurisdiction of the Dominion Railway Board and the Interstate Commerce Commission. I refer to the hand-grips on
box cars. It becomes second nature to a railway man in the dead of night, without stopping to look, to reach to a certain place to take hold of the hand-grip on a freight car; and if it is not there, he may get under the wheels. I repeat that you cannot get uniformity unless you have uniformity of control. Railway employees as a body have been working long and arduously to get this enactment into the railway law, so that the Railway Board will have jurisdiction and will know that the equipment is uniform. They do not want to interfere with the right of a province in its own railway, but they do want the large body to have jurisdiction over the smaller one,

I endorse absolutely what has been said by my hon. friend (Mr. G. B. Nicholson). The very matter that he has referred to is what gave rise-to the amendment. In 1913 complaints were made to the board with regard to the operation of the Quebec Central railway, which was under a 999-year lease to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Application was made for the establisment of uniformity of devices, appliances and so on.
What has been done here is to pass a law so that where any provincial road is owned, controlled, leased, or operated by a company wholly or partly within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, the provincial company shall also be within the provisions of the Railway Act and subject to the jurisdiction of the Dominion Railway Board. In that way uniformity in devices will be obtained. If what is suggested by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) were adopted, and at the end of the lease the company went back to the regulations which obtained in any province they might be quite different, for instance, the devices on box cars, which have bden referred to, and accidents would be almost certain to result. It is for that purpose that this clause is inserted. It is really for the protection of railway employees.

If you take the case of a smaller road which has operated for a number of years with a larger road, for instance if you take the case of the Quebec Central, you will find that its equipment is just the same as that of the Canadian Pacific. It could not couple its cars with those of the Canadian Pacific if it did not have the same coupling device. To have different equipment would restrict the trade of the company and make it an absolute failure. Business interests would compel it to have the same equipment. All these new devices

must be used, because it would be suicidal for such a company not to have them.
We need not worry about the Quebec Central, because it is under lease to the Canadian Pacific for 999 years and will continue to be operated by that company.

I object to the principle that we should bind forever a company which is at present under a certain management. This control ought not to go beyond the time mentioned in the agreement, [f a company is subject to provincial legislative powers, let it be so; but if it amalgamates with a federal company, I am willing that, for the time of the amalgamation, it should be subject to Federal jurisdiction, but when that agreement expires, why impose upon that company the necessity of remaining where perhaps, it would not like to be?
The company can come to the Parliament of the day and get relief.

Why force it to come to Parliament?	-
MrrNESBITT: It might be better for it.

We are not here to do guess work for the welfare of other people who are supposed to look into the matter of their incorporation when they become incorporated. This is a question that affects future interests of people who Are not bound by any agreement. When this agreement has expired by the lapse of time, you force them to remain in a condition to which they did not want to submit before they came to make this agreement and which was imposed upon them by the making of the agreement.
We did not force it upon them.

Is it impossible to use other language than the language used here? The objectionable part is the clause "for the general advantage of Canada." No matter how small a property may be, if it is entirely within a province, when you declare it to be for the general advantage of Canada, it will be very awkward to be obliged some day to come back to Parliament for legislation declaring that it is not for the general advantage of Canada, and that 'is the only way to get back to the former itatus. It would be a very peculiar piece-of legislation to put through this House,
fMr. Bureau.!
to declare that a certain piece of property was not for the general advantage of Canada. If the language was used that this road while so operated shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the board, then when the owner got the property hack, he would be no longer subject to the jurisdiction of the board. In that way, you would have the same effect, but the property would not be forever declared to be property within Dominion jurisdiction.
Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.

I would ask the permission of the Committee to draw attention to a matter which properly would come under clause 8. Before I really understood the procedure of the Committee, I had allowed this clause to slip by. It has been carried, and I have to ask the permission of the Committee to speak to it.

That is satisfactory.
On motion of Mr. H. A. Mackie, the Committee reverted to the consideration of clause 8.	.
On clause 8.-provincial railways connecting with or crossing Dominion railways:

Under this -clause the question of crossings arises, and a case may very will be imagined, indeed, a case has occurred where some difficulty has been apprehended in the matter of crossings and the meaning and definition of " crossings ", where, for instance, a railway company operating or about to operate under a provincial -charter has a certain location route and another -company operating under a Dominion charter had virtually the .same route and they came into conflict. A case has arisen in Alberta between the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific. The Canadian Northerh had. a provincial charter and the Canadian Pacific a Dominion charter. The lines of the two railways as shown by their respective location plans.- though at different levels-both cross each other and also join each other .so as to run along much the same right-of-way at .several places, in what the plaintiff's counsel designates the -"confliction area." The case was tried .and decided by a .single judge, which decision is. not by any means binding, .and it might be profitable for the Committee to have a better definition of what is meant by the word " crossing," .so as to. cover a case where roads are not in operation. The learned judge in that case said:

In my opinion, that section has no application to the case in hand. It seems to me that the evidence establishes a case substantially of both companies claiming a right to build upon the same right-of-way and that at different levels ; that one railway " joining " another means joining on the same level so as to enable cars to be transferred from the tracks of one road to the tracks of another; and that " crossing " means the passing of the tracks of one railway on, over or under the tracks of another by meeting at any angle, continuing at the same angle to the opposite side of j:he track crossed and immediately leaving the track crossed.
The question taken before the court was this: " Is there any question of crossing any track or level inasmuch as neither railway cqmpany has thought of construction or operation?" The judge comes to the conclusion that it is merely a question of the right of a Dominion Parliament charter having precedence over a charter of the province. He says:
To he concrete, the Dominion Parliament has exclusive legislative authority with respect to the Canadian Pacific Railway Co., the defendant company y and the Legislature of the province of Alberta exclusive legislature authority with respect to the Canadian Northern Western Railway Co., the plaintiff company. These legislative bodies, while each exercising its apparently exclusive jurisdiction, have conferred, each upon its own creature, powers apparently equal and a conflict has arisen.	-
The decision of the court was that where, as in this case, there is a conflict of rights granted by two different authorities, the authority granted by the Dominion Parliament is supreme. I submit that some amendment ought to be made to make it clear that where railways have secured authority from different sources and a conflict arises, the right granted by the Dominion Parliament shall have precedence over the rights granted by any other legislative authority.

I think the section
already provides that.

That is what we intended to provide.
Mr. H. A. MA'CKIE: It may be that it does, but I cannot see it, and I shall be very glad if one of the members of the Railway Committee will point out where this provision is.

I think paragraph (a)
of section 8 covers the point raised by my hon. friend, and if it is in any way deficient I should like him- to point it out.
Progress reported.

PRINCE OF WALES TO VISIT CANADA.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE OF WALES TO VISIT CANADA.
speechtext:
I have the honour to announce the text of a message from His Majesty the King to His Excellency the Governor General, as follows:
I am very glad to tell you that with my entire approval the Prince of Wales will visit Canada this year leaving England in August. He will open the new Parliament Buildings in Ottawa.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock and again went into Committee on Bill No. 19, to consolidate and amend the Railway Act, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

The hon. member
for North Perth says that section 8 covers the point under discussion. The section says:
Every railway, the construction or operation of which is authorized by special Act of the legislature of any province, and which connects with or crosses or may hereafter connect with or cross any railway within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, shall-	'
-and so on. Under this section it is assumed that the railway is in operation or has been constructed or partly constructed. It does not contemplate railways on which no work has been done. The case I was dealing with is this. A railway company gets a charter from the province under the Provincial Railway Act and does everything necessary preparatory to the construction of its road. Another company is incorporated under the Dominion Railway Act, and it also complies with the requirements preparatory to the construction of its road. One company begins construction, and in doing so encroaches upon some territory or route that the other company, which we may call the plaintiff company, purposes to operate under the provincial charter. There is a conflict between the two. The routes cross and re-cross and at some point the defendant company constructs exactly on the same route that the plaintiff company had in view. The plaintiff company in this case seeks an injunction to restrain the defendant from constructing over a certain portion of its proposed route, because the

plaintiff, by provincial charter, claims exclusive jurisdiction. The defendant company claims that it has a perfect right to construct wherever it sees fit because it holds authority from the Dominion Parliament. The defendant says: "You have done nothing; you are not operating and have not even constructed; we have begun first and are entitled to priority, notwithstanding the conflict of rights between us. Take the case brought before the courts of Alberta, in which the Canadian Northern Railway seeks an injunction against the Canadian Pacific. Under Section 227 of the old Act it is provided:-
The railway lines or tracks of any company shall not cross or join, or be crossed or joined by or with any railway lines or tracks other than those of such company whether otherwise within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada or not until leave therefore has been obtained 'from the board as hereinafter provided.
The judgment in the case says:-*
In my opinion, that section has no application to the case in hand. It seems to me that the evidence establishes a case substantially of both companies claiming a right to build upon the same right-of-way and that at different
levels. ,	,	:
" Joining" means joining on the same level, and " crossing " the passing of tracks *of one railway over or under the tracks of another by meeting at any angle, continuing at the [DOT]same angle to the opposite side of the track crossed, and immediately leaving the track crossed. The judgment proceeds:-
The proper conclusion is, I think, that to this extent at least and speaking generally, Dominion railway legislation prima facie predominates over .provincial railway legislation, that Parliament in legislating in relation to Dominion railways may as far as may be reasonably necessary to effect the object of its legislation impose obligations upon a provincial railway, that where Parliament has legislated with relation to a Dominion railway-as ilt has by the Railway Act and the defendent company's charter-what it has enacted cannot be derogated from by provincial legislature, and consequently had I thought it necessary for the decision of the questions involved in this action to have expressed an opinion upon S. 227 of The (Dominion) Railway Act with regard to crossings and junctions, I shiouild have held both that it wa!s within the power of the Dominion Parliament and also that it purported to and did apply to a provincial railway.
I have saiid that it seems to me, speaking generally, a Dominion railway will have predominating rights over a provincial railway, prima facie: wihat I mean to imply is that all other things1 being equal the predominance is not to be doubted ibut that the subsequent history of either railway may perhaps give the provincial railway a status which can be interfered with only, if at all, to a restricted extent.

Idington, J., in one of his judgments, says:-
The Dominion Parliament having by virtue of its exclusive powers over the enumerated subjects in sea 91 of the B.N.A. Act created a corporate power and thereby conferred on one or more persons the power to construct or cause to he constructed a railway, that rail-1 way cannot be crossed by any other railway company which, with its work, is only the product of the somewhat analogous powers given by section 92 to provincial legislatures over "local works and undertakings."
I am with great respect, quite unable to understand how any express and exclusive dominating power such as given by the Act to the Dominion Parliament despite the so-called exclusive authority subject thereto given to the province is ever in any case to be minimized, much less deleted from the Act, because of some apparently inconsistent power given to the provinces. If need be to discard either, it is the subsequent and subordinate power that must, be deleted as it were, in order to give the precedent and paramount power its full effective operation.	'	.
in conclusion, the judgment says:
I am of opinion, therefore, that the plaintiff company, in its present condition at least of being an unconstructed railway, can in no way interfere, with the construction of the defendant company's railway.
There seems to be the same difficulty in the way when both railways are umcon-structed. That is the decision of an Alberta judge. This does not make the matter final. Rather than have any repetition of lawsuits on this very, point, I ask Parliament to make it clear, under this or any other section, that where there is a conflict between the .provincial and Dominion legislatures in the granting of powers to railway companies which have not constructed and net operated, the authority given by the Dominion Parliament shall predominate over the power given by the legislature. That is the whole point at issue and one that has already caused some litigation. It is easy to understand how a company having a Dominion charter, if it is necessary to obtain even the consent of the board to cross a certain route or line to be constructed, receives that consent and the Dominion Government has no knowledge that a provincial legislature has given the same authority to another company over the same ground. Why not do away with conflict in a case of that sort? Section 8, or any other section which may he subordinated to it, only deals with railways when in operation or constructed, or which al least have done something towards construction or operation, I believe that answers the objection of the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) and I hope I have made my point clear.

I am still in the dark, and I hope to convince my hon. friend that this Bill gives a complete answer to his contention. Without Te-quoting section 8, I will just read the first two words: "Every railway The Bill does not say " every constructed railway ". To get the hieaning of the term " railway " I refer to the interpretation clause of section 2, subsection 21, which defines the meaning of the word " railway
" Railway " means any railway which the company has authority to construct or operate-
Not " has constructed " or " has oper- _ ated ", as my hon. friend has argued, not that has been partly constructed or .operated, but any railway which may thereafter be constructed.
Under this Act?

Yes, under this Act.
-and includes all branches, extensions, sidings, depots, wharvesetc. Section 8 provides that the Dominion jurisdiction is paramount to the provincial. Section 8 operates generally and applies to all railways under a provincial or federal charter whether they are constructed or unconstructed. It seems to be so clear that I cannot conceive of any court having any difficulty in the reading of the section.
Has the definition of " railway " been altered as compared with the definition in the last Act?

If any judge on this reading gave the decision which the hon. gentleman says was given, I think' he must have given that decision without having looked at the interpretation clause as it is in the Act. No judge could give such a decision if this wording were there.
On section 10-Chief Commissioner and Assistant Chief Commissioner:

I move:
That section 10, subsection 2, lines 1 and 2, be amended by striking out the words " or assistant chief commissioner " and inserting a new subsection between sections 2 and 3 as subsection 2 (a) :
" (2a) Any person may be appointed Assistant Chief Commissioner who is or has been a judge of a superior court of Canada or of any province of Canada, or who is a barrister of at least ten years' standing at the bar of any such province, or who is a barrister or advocate of any such province and has held office as a Commissioner of the Board for a period of at least ten years."
The object of the change is merely to say that if it is thought advisable a person
who has been a commissioner for ten years, although not a barrister for ten years, may be promoted to be assistant chief commissioner. It really means that Mr. McLean may be appointed to fill the position of assistant 'chief commissioner.
Mr. MoMASTER:	I note that in the
tenth line you say " who is a barrister or advocate " while in the ninth line, you merely use the word " barrister." I think it would be well to say " barrister or advocate " in both cases.

There is no objection
to adding the word " advocate " in the ninth line.

What is the necessity
of putting in " advocate." Is there any difference between a barrister and an advocate? There is not in our province.

I do not see any great necessity at all.
Mr. iMcMASTER:	You have used the
word "'advocate " in one case and you say " barrister or advocate " in the other. I quite agree with my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie). "Barrister" and " advocate " mean the same thing in the province of Quebec. I would suggest that you either strike out the word " advocate " or insert it in both cases?

I think it would be
better to strike out " or advocate " in the tenth line. I would therefore move:
That the words " or advocate " be stricken out.
Amendment agreed to.

I do not quite understand the effect of the last two lines.
" or who is a barrister of any such province and has held office as a commissioner of the Board for a period of at least ten years.
If you stop at " province " is that not all you require?

I believe that has been added because Mr. McLean is not a barrister of ten years standing. ing a caveat. This is merely to meet the ' requirements of registration in the western provinces.

by caveat.

Is there not a provision in the Railway Act for notice by caveat as stated by the hon. gentleman? If there is, the wording suggested would be unfortunate. The clause seems very plain and comprehensive in itself.

This is the Alberta law:	An agreement for sale, mortgage or
any agreement of whatever nature it may be, with the exception of an absolute transfer, cannot be registered except by caveat. That caveat is drawn up and a notice something like this is filed in the Registrar's office:
Take notice that so-and-so declares that he has *a claim against a certain property under an agreement for sale, or under a mortgage or under any other documentary Evidence. That notice is filed and that is the only means we have of registering the interest that a man may have. "Under the clause as it stands we have no way of getting notice to anybody, unless provision is made for notice by way of caveat. The registrar will accept that notice and he will stamp it upon the record which contains a description of the land in question, and nobody can deal with that land until the registrar removes that notice of caveat. In Alberta that is the only way in which a man who has an interest less than an absolute interest in a piece of land can protect, his interest.
