On section 232-appeal from award:

What I was endeavouring to point out under subsection (13) of section 2 was that a judge appointed as arbitrator who granted an order or gave a direction in any proceedings taken under the arbitration was acting as a person desig-

nated, and not as a judge of the oourt, and that if an appeal were taken from this interlocutory measure, if I may so call it, a . legal question of very great difficulty would arise. I was unable this afternoon to convince the Committee by my own exposition of the case, and I shall now endeavour to convince it by a judgment of the court. In the case of Marsan vs. the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, reported in the Alberta Law Reports 1909, volume 2, the judge says-'(page 43):
Quaere-Whether or not the judgment of a judge who is persona designata is appealable in view of the decision in C.P.R. vs. Little Seminary of Ste. Therese, since the enactment of s. 220 of the Railway Act.
Qusere-Whether or not a dissatisfied litigant who has the right to appeal must appeal and is not at liberty to bring the same matter before the Court in a different way.
Held, that where the right of appeal was doubtful and the plaintiff had given notice of appeal, and at the same time brought an action for injunction, in which action the validity of the order appealed from would have to be inquired into, the matter was properly before the Court.
Secondly, from the same judgment I read:
Where there is a failure to comply with the Act the jurisdiction of the judge is wanting, and the company may be restrained from acting under a warrant granted. The warrants in question-
These are warrants for possession of land.
-if these appeals were granted by Mr. Justice Beck under and in pursuance of the power given in section 217 and 218 of the Railway Act and the learned judge in granting such warrants acted persona designata and there can be no appeal from his decision: C.P.R. vs. Little Seminary of Ste. Therese, and particularly the language of Mr. Justice Patterson, p. 618.
Mr. Justice Stuart says:
.With respect to the appeal from the order of Mr. Justice Beck directing the warrant of possession to issue, the preliminary objection was taken by council for the respondent company, that Mr. Justice Beck was acting as persona designata in making the order, and that, therefore, in accordance with the decision in The Canadian Pacific Railway Company vs. The Little Seminary of Ste. Therese, there is no right of appeal. There may be some doubt as to whether this case is now binding upon us in view of the subsequent insertion of section 220 into the Railway Act, but inasmuch as the plaintiff has in fact appealed from the order granting the warrants, and has brought his actions for injunctions as well, it is clear that the whole matter is now properly before us, either in the one form or the other.
The point I have been endeavouring to make is this: Some company may want possession of land, as in the case I have cited. They go to a judge and say: " Give us a warrant for possession." The respondent
company says: "You have no right to the possession of this land because you have not fulfilled all the requirements of the Railway Act." An injunction is sought, and notice of appeal is given from the judgment granting the warrant. Then when action is taken on the basis of the warrant granted you have a double remedy before the courts: First, the notice of appeal that you have given, and, secondly, an action for damages for trespass, whether nominal or actual. One of the litigants will tell you at once:
" You cannot seek damages by way of injunction because you have given notice of appeal." The other litigant says: " When the judge gave you this warrant he was acting as persona designata and you cannot appeal from his decision." That was the case I put before the Committee this afternoon, and I ask that subsection 13 of section 2 be amended to make it clear that when a judge gives suoh an order as giving a warrant for possession or directs notice to be served these orders aie orders of the court, and not merely the orders of a man who stands in the position of an arbitrator.
To further convince the Committee of the ambiguity of the law, let me cite another case, Saunders vs. the Edmonton and Dun vegan Railway, and we may see how other judges look at this question. In the case I cited a moment ago I was dealing both with a single judge and the Appellant Division, but in this case you have other judges of the Appellant Division sitting, and observe how they disagree with the judgment given in the Marsan case:-
By virtue of section 220, the Railway Act, eh. 37, R.S.C., a judge in granting a warrant of possession under sec. 217 to a railway company is acting as a judge.
A full court^in Marsan vs. the Grand Trunk Pacific held that the judge was acting as an arbitrator, was persona des'ignata. In this case the full court, but not the same personnel, holds that he is acting as a judge.
The report says:
By virtue of sec. 220, the Railway Act, ch. .37, R.S.C., a judge in granting a warrant of possession under sec. 217, to a railway company is acting as a Judge of the Court and not as a persona designata; Canadian Pacific Ry. Co. vs. The Little Seminary of Ste. Therese, 16, S.C.R., 606, distinguished. The grant of such a warrant is, therefore, subject to appeal.
A warrant of possession granted under sec. 217, the Railway Act, ch. 37, R.S.C., by a judge of general jurisdiction is effective for the purposes intended until set aside in the regular way, and the fact that there has been a failure to comply with some of the statutory provisions does not render the warrant void, but merely irregular.

The Chief Justice in delivering his portion of the judgment in the case says:
The plaintiff by his statement of claim alleges that he was in August, 1912, the owner in possession of certain lands and that at that time the defendants " wrongfully and unlawfully entered upon the said lands " and did certain damage. He claims (1) Damages for the wrongful acts complained of; (2) An injunction; (3) In the alternative if the railway is authorized to be constructed through the lands, damages for the land taken and to the remaining land.
The defendants deny the plaintiff's allegations and set up that they went upon the land in pursuance of a warrant of possession duly obtained from a judge of the Supreme Court. Plaintiff joins issue	
Even if it is open to the plaintiff under the pleadings to test the validity of the warrant of possession, which is doubtful, I am of opinion that he has failed in his attack upon it. He contends that the judge in making it is acting as a persona designata and that any failure to comply with the express provisions of the Act would result in rendering his act a mere nullity.
I do not need to take time to read the contradictory opinions of judges in this matter. Assuming for the sake of argument that the legal talent of this House say that the decisions I have read provide that you may take action and bring before the courts of your province the very subject matter of the order about which you would take an appeal, and that consequently whether you have the right of appeal or not you are still at liberty' to take an action for nominal trespass, why should a man on a legal question be obliged to take a double remedy-first to file a notice of appeal from a decision of a single judge arbitrator, who in one case is not a judge and in another case is admitted to he a judge? Why should he be put to all, the trouble of taking action to maintain the very point he could maintain if he hqd a proper case for appeal? I hope that' I have made it clear that section 232 deals only with the appeal from an award, and does not provide any machinery by which you can appeal in cases such as I have cited. In conjunction with this matter I may call attention to section 243 which says:
-and where there are different interests in the same lands all shall as far as possible be dealt with in one proceeding.
These sections should be taken jointly, because often a judge, if acting in that capacity, could settle by an order of the court the claims of any one of the litigants, whereas now, no matter what may be the attitude of the litigants, it must all be decided in the one proceeding as far as possible. It is of the greatest importance,

I contend, in view of the contradictory decisions that have been given in our province in this matter, that the law should be made clear whether a judge is acting simply as an arbitrator or as a judge of court. This brings me back to section 2, paragraph (13). Even if- you amended section 232, the courts would immediately turn to the interpretation clause, and if they held under it that "judge" meant a judge arbitrator and not a judge of the court, all that you might say in section 232 would be of no use. So that if an amendment is to be made in section 232 there must also be an amendment in paragraph (13) in section 2.	.

We had quite a discussion in connection with section 232, and I think perhaps it is better to leave it as it is. There is an appeal in a case of award for compensation where the amount is over $600. In other cases where it is necessary for a railway company to take possession of lands they apply to the judge for authority to enter, and the judge granting such authority is acting as an arbitrator. In such a case there is no appeal. The judge can issue an order giving the railway company power to enter and take possession of lands, and that order is final. But after possession is taken, if the party from whom the land is taken is not satisfied with the amount of the award he can appeal to a higher court, if the amount exceeds $600. If a railway company wishing to start construction work could not begin until their right to take possession had been considered by various courts they would be greatly disadvantaged. From the decision of the judge who gave authority to take possession there might be an appeal from one court to another and the railway would never get possession of the lands or be able to build its railway. This clause empowers the judge, -who may be an arbitrator, to give authority to enter and take possession, and as regards compensation the owner can appeal. The judge decides the question of possession, and the compensation is disposed of afterwards.

The angle from
which the minister views the matter is altogether different from my viewpoint. It is true that under the Railway Act. which is now before Parliament if a judge grants an order for possession and he is wrong you may move at once that the party who got the warrant of possession shall deposit in the court a certain amount of security. That is provided for in the Railway Act.

There is no harm done in so far as the ultimate result of the case is concerned, but in so far as the man who is to receive the money is concerned there is, because the court can order the issue of a warrant of possession and also issue an order for security, but this entails unnecessary costs. But the point I have made is that if something is irregularly done or without jurisdiction by >a judge, I have no appeal under the law as it is interpreted by the court .at the present time. That it has been on the Statute Book from time immemorial is no reason why it should remain on the Statute Book. It is only creating trouble in the carrying out of the Act. 1 am not merely raising a legal point but my object is to avoid litigation. Apparently the policy of the Government is to foster litigation. I am a barrister and I would like to have a lot of work .but where difficulties arise, such as have' arisen, and when judges hold contradictory opinions, why not settle it at once? It is just a question whether a judge is acting as a judge of a court or is acting as an arbitrator. If he is acting as an arbitrator I have no redress except to take an action at law, and as the basis of my action I must allege trespass which will mean a nominal fifty cents and costs. Why should my client be put to all that trouble? I should simply have to file notice of appeal to the full court and the case is -decided on the merits, or on legal questions, before the court, and if there are any costs incurred it would be the costs of appeal and any court is in a position to deal with costs and to decide as to whether a warrant of possession may properly be given or not. I am not dealing at all with the question from the angle of the minister that no harm can ensue from this section, because if a warrant of possession is' given a man has his recourse and he can get his money. A man who has got irregularly a warrant of possession may be forced to give security in the courts. Why should a company be permitted to go before any judge in the country and get a warrant of pdssession on affidavits which are not correct? Why should it be that under such circumstances I should -have no relief except to take a straight action at law and put my clients to all sorts of trouble? Why should a company be allowed to take advantage of such irregularity for the purpose of proceeding with the construction of a line? Our purpose is to see that the Railway Act is lived up to. I had a conversation with a minister yesterday and he said that he would see that the law's of the country were
obeyed. I told him that I would do the same thing. I am asking that the laws of the country be obeyed and that no railway company be allowed to start'the operation or construction of any railway on the strength of a warrant of possession' obtained from a judge on affidavits Which are not correct. I have no remedy except to tell my client that he must take a straight action and claim trespass, the result of which may secure him $1 and costs. That is a condition of things that I have proven here, not only by my own exposition, which is not very clear, but rather by quoting from the judgments of the courts. Now is the time to make the law right, and there is no reason why this Committee cannot go back to subsection (13) of section 2 and say that when we speak of a judge, we speak of a judge having the power of a court. If we do that, it would settle the whole situation.

I think the clause should remain as it is. We must take it for granted that the judges are men of common sense- they are as a rule-and that they are not going to issue these warrants without fully considering the case. It is to the advantage of the country that there should be as few appeals as possible. The minister has put the business side of it in a very clear manner, and I do not think that is a different angle from that from which it has been viewed by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Mackie). The section says that a company should not be held up, but that the ultimate result will be to do justice as between the land owner and the company. My hon. friend does not suggest an amendment here, but he wants the law made so clear that there can be no appeal. I venture to say that we cannot so frame the law that there will be no appeal.
What time have I had to prepare an amendment when the motion is made to-night that we go into Committee,at once and no notice is given that we are going into Committee?

If my hon. friend even had time to prepare an amendment I do not think he could prepare one which could resist the ingenuity of the bar of Alberta to get by the statute. My hon. friend has proved to us apparently that even the courts of his own province differ as to whether the word "judge" means qua judge or a judge as persona designata. Apparently the Superior Court of Alberta has held that he is sitting as a judge. It is stated in sub-

section (13) of section 2 that "judge" is a judge of the Superior or county court.
It would be far better to leave it at that and have the law construed under the ordinary canons of interpretation that he is a judge. If any particular case should arise of that kind, which I doubt now in view of the decision of the appellate division of Alberta, or if a judge should be held not to have power, which is very doubtful, let that case take care of itself. Anybody who has studied the railway law and the cases in Canada knows that it is a case of the most extraordinary rarity that any dispute has been had as to the warrant of a judge ordering possession. We would be going out of our way if we tried to make an amendment to cover the extremely rare case that the hon. gentleman has cited here. It would probably result in an increase in ligitation on the part of ingenious litigants or their counsel and we would be no better off than before. I think the clause should be left as it is.

On section 346-Members of Parliament and Board, etc., free:
Why are not judges of the Supreme Court of Canada, and of the superior courts, county courts and district courts for the several provinces included in this clause?

The Railway Act has
never provided for judges being given free transportation. There is no particular reason why they should travel free. On the contrary, judges must go on circuit and their travelling expenses while on circuit are paid by the province. If we were to give the judges free passes it would mean that the provinces would be getting the benefit except, of course when judges were travelling for private reasons. I cannot see why the railways should be deprived of this source of revenue.

In Canada, but in no other part of the British Empire, the. judges are treated as magnified civil servants, and are underpaid. While they get their travelling expenses on circuit refunded, they are not free to travel to and fro throughout the Dominion as they should be permitted to do, in order that they might have an opportunity of learning how the different provinces conduct their law courts. I think the judges should be given an annual pass over all the railways.

I quite agree that the judges are not receiving sufficiently high salaries, but the only way to remedy that is for Parliament to vote them a higher salary. I cannot see why we should expect the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National Railways to help pay the salaries of our judges by giving them free passes. We should be big enough to pay them adequate salaries ourselves. Although the judges are not receiving adequate salaries, I might say that ever since I have been a member of the Government I have never found any difficulty in getting a man to accept a judgeship when one became vacant. We should appoint to the Bench the very best men we can get, and we cannot get the very best men at the salaries we are paying to-day. I believe that in some cases the result is that people probably do not get the judgments they would if we were able to appoint the very best judges. But I do not think we should discuss the salaries of judges on this Bill.

I will give a reason why they should be granted travelling passes. Historically and traditionally the judges should stand between the legislative body and the people. If there are a number of men chasing after judgeships it is because of the way in which the appointments are made. In the province of Alberta to-day there are three judgeships vacant, and twelve politicians looking for judgeships. So long as judgeships are granted principally for political services rendered, rather than upon a man's record at the Bar, just so long you will not be able to get the best men in the country to sit on the Bench.

I understand that the Government is considering the question of increasing the salaries of the judges.
I think the reason advanced by the hon. member for Edmonton for granting passes to judges is a fallacious one. If judges should be allowed to travel on the railways free to see how court business is conducted
in other portions of the Dominion, you should extend the same privilege to sohool teachers, for instance. The whole principle is wrong.

On section 376, subsection (7)-Connections with other systems, power of board to order:
Why were the words "including compensation if any", in subsection (7), in line 29, not struck out?
We are now on section 376. We made no changes in it.

I move to amend subsection (7), of section 376 by striking out the words "including compensation if any" in line 29, and adding thereto the following:
Provided however that the charge to such first-mentioned company, province, municipality or corporation for any long distance conversation or message transmitted over a line owned, controlled or operated hy the company shall not be more than the established long distance rate of the company.

We had a considerable discussion in the Committee in regard to this and went into the matter thoroughly, and the Committee decided that the clause as it is now and as it has been in the ,Bill should remain.
'Mr. CASGRAIN:	Is this amendment
,made at the request or suggestion of the

Bell Telephone Company or any other company?

We are not moving
the amendment; it is moved by the hon. member for York (Mr. Wallace). I do not know at whose instance it is moved.
, Mr. FIELDING: Perhaps the hon. member might explain the amendment. Those present at the discussion in the Committee will understand it, but to many hon. members the striking out of a few words will pot convey any clear meaning.

Is it for the purpose of
.restricting the jurisdiction of the Board and determining the terms upon which connections shall be made?
It is to provide that the Bell or any other telephone company shall not have power over independent telephones.

I understand that when
a small company want to connect with a larger system, if they cannot agree upon the terms they shall go before the Board, who shall determine the terms and conditions upon which they shall connect, and determine conmpensation, if any. What is the object of striking out the words " including compensation if any"? Is it to eliminate compensation, even if there is a right to it?

This was very fully discussed in the Committee. Certain persons desired to eliminate these words, " including compensation if any," because they claimed that no compensation should be allowed. The majority of the Committee decided that it would be better to leave it to the board to decide if compensation should be allowed.
That is what the clause does now?

Exactly. It was argued by the majority of the committee that if these words were eliminated the board would not have power to allow any compensation, no matter what the conditions were or how deserving the case. Therefore, the committee decided to leave these words in.
After discussing the matter?
After an exhaustive discussion for days.

What is the object of the amendment? If you strike out the words " including compensation if any " you limit

the powers of the board. Supposing there is any damage done we prevent the board from assessing the damages. Is that the object?

I think I understand what the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace) means. There is a strong feeling which he represents here, I understand, that users of the Bell telephone should have the same right to use their long distance lines as if they were subscribers, although they are subscribers to a private line. The way the law is now, and with the words " including compensation if any," there is an addition to tne rates of the Bell Telephone company. It amounts to $600 in some cases where there are over 400 subscribers to a local line. It was thought that was too much of a burden to put on the users of the local telephone lines, and that all local telephone users should have tne right to connect up with the Bell without paying that extra compensation.
We decide, without hearing the merits of the case, that whether or not any company is entitled to compensation they shall not have compensation?

That is what it
means.

I think that is rather arbitrary, and I would not like to vote for anything of that kind. I think it would be better to leave it to the decision of the board after hearing the evidence. Unless there is some further explanation given I cannot see my way clear to support the amendment..

I do not see why the
words " including compensation if any " should be in at all. " Upon such terms, as the hoard shall direct " ought to he sufficient. The inclusion of the words " such compensation if any" lends colour to the argument that compensation was intended. We had a case before the committee. I think it was the case of the Ingersoll Telephone company. This company had a large number of phones and sent about six times as much business to the Bell company as they got from it. It was a great advantage to the company. Many other companies would also do that. There are many small companies, some of them struggling to get along, sending business to the Bell company which is much more valuable to the Bell than the short distance connection is to themselves and to put in this section, " including compensation " and then after it the words " if any " carries with it the implication that compensation may be
168i
asked for. Compensation for what? For handing over revenues that the Bell would not otherwise get if they were not connected with the local company? I think the words " compensation if any " should be left out and that the section should read " upon such terms as the board deems just and expedient." That would be a fair clause. The question of compensation is not directly placed before the board to be dealt with.
Do you mean that it is a suggestion to the board that might. influence them?

Yes. I think in a way it might possibly be so. It certainly would not suggest anything by way of compensation if the words were not there. Why put them in when you have the words " such terms and conditions as to the board may seem just and expedient?"
The hon. member (Mr. Morphy) was a member of the committee and recalls the discussion we had about the very point he has raised.

Yes, I took the same
ground there.

My hon. friend took
the same ground there. We went into the question very thoroughly and the majority of the committee decided that we should have these words in the clause. I think the elause should pass as it is here because this matter is left entirely in the hands of the board and they can take up each case and do justice to all parties concerned.

I would like to explain this clause a little bit because I have been very much mixed up with this question the last few years. When the House of Commons passed this clause in 1917 they sent it to the Senate after striking out the words "including compensation." In the old Railway Act the words "including compensation" appeared. The Senate inserted', the words "including compensation if any." They added the two little words "if any" to the words "including compensation" which had appeared in the old Act.
Mr. MeKENZIE:	They continued the
language of the old Act?

Yes, and added the words "if any" so as to make it clear that it was not necessary to give compensation unless it was thought to be justified. Lawyers argued before the Committee that under the old Act containing the words "including compensation" the board necessarily had to give compensation because those

words implied that compensation was to be allowed, but, that the addition of the words "if any" removed the obligation to give compensation. The Bell company did not charge compensation to those rural companies who were not competitors in cities, towns and villages but they did charge compensation where rural companies were competitors, for the reason, as they say, that the rural company takes away a certain number of their subscribers. Therefore they claim they vshould have compensation. I moved in 1917 that the words "including compensation" be struck out. That was carried in the Commons Committee at that time but the Senate put the words in again and added "if any" so as to leave it to the board, which made it better than it was before in my judgment. You have to bear in mind that the Bell company impose on the rural companies a charge over and above the regular rates and that is what the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace) is trying to get at by his amendment. They make a charge generally of about ten cents over and above the regular rates against the rural company connecting with them. That surcharge is generally divided half and half, but in some cases it is not so. At Ingersoll the Bell company get 7 cents and the Ingersoll company 3 cents, but they charge the Ingersoll company compensation to the extent of $300 because that company com-' petes with them in the town of Ingersoll.
That is why at that time I moved that that be struck out, because, speaking offhand, they derived from the Ingersoll company about $1,100 one year and about $1,300 another year, while the Ingersoll company only got about $189 one year and less than that the next year. For that reason the rural companies-and they were here by the flock before the Committee^, claimed that compensation should not be allowed to the Bell company, a good many of them, also claimed that they should not be charged a surcharge. That was not listened to very favourably by the Committee, I confess, because they thought the Bell company should have something for the additional expense.
Some of them.

But as it passed the Committee I have nothing further to say about the matter. I moved at the time that that be struck out, I was defeated, and I am willing to take my defeat and abide by the decision of the majority. So far as Ingersoll is concerned, in 1917 the total earnings
[iMr. Nesbitt.]
on surcharges were $1,632.09, of which the Bell company got $1,T43 and the Ingersoll company $189, the latter company being charged $300 for the compensation.
For the privilege of giving a big revenue to the Bell company.
I have explained as nearly as I can the position that was taken throughout on this clause, and I repeat, having been defeated by the Committee I am wdll-ing to abide by my defeat.

I think the member for West York (Mr. Wallace) is right: There should be no compensation, there should be reciprocity in a matter of this kind. The member speaks of the Bell company feeling aggrieved because some of their business was taken away. That would not have happened had they been reasonable with those who wished to use the telephone. The Bell company virtually made it impossible for the rural population to take their telephone service. Now that company comes along and wants compensa-* tion to the extent of thousands of dollars throughout the province. It is one of the greatest monopolies and I think the Committee would be quite justified in striking this clause out. The Bell company ought to be satisfied with what it gets and encourage reciprocity with outside telephone companies.

We had a similar fight when this Bill went through the House before, and after discussing it until two o'clock in the morning, the Committee struck the clause out. Of course, the hon. Senate saw fit to [DOT] reinstate the words. I think the Bell Company have already a sufficient monopoly without allowing them to extort this compensation. I know municipal systems with hundreds of subscribers in country districts which the Bell Company refused accommodation, and if any subscriber on those systems required to use long distance, the Bell Company insisted on payment of the regular long distance charge and ten cents extra. Why should a man outside the city of Ottawa, if he happens to be on a municipal or privately-owned system, have to pay the Bell Company ten cents more than the Bell subscriber in the city of Ottawa, or a fereigner, if you like, coming in from another country? I think it is a preposterous position. In the meantime those municipal and privately-owned rural systems are bringing in thousands of dollars

to the Bell Company, and yet that company wants to penalize these systems.

" Upon such terms, including compensation, if any, as the board deems just and expedient, and may order and direct how, when, where, by whom and upon what terms and conditions such use, connection or communication shall be had, constructed, installed, operated and maintained." If a rural line makes application to the Bell Company for a connection, and they cannot agree on terms, they have a right to appeal to the Board of Railway Commissioners, and the board has absolute power to compel the Bell Company to make that connection on this clause as it stands. I do not think that is where the complaint is; it is more as to compensation. I do not think that the question of compensation would arise in very many instances, but in any event a clause such as this protects all concerned, and we all have confidence in the Board of Railway Commissioners.
What have the courts said?

I do not know what the courts may have said in the past. But I understand that this clause gives the Board the final decision, with the reservation, of course, that in all cases there is a right of appeal from the Board to the Governor in Council. The Board can order that connection free of charge if it sees fit to do so, and of course the Act is framed entirely on the understanding that we have confidence in the Board of Railway Commissioners.
Will the minister explain why there should be any compensation at all?

I do not say there
should be compensation if, for instance, it is merely a connection with a rural line. But, if I remember rightly, in the discussion before the Committee, cases were brought to our attention where there might be compensation. For instance, the Bell Company 'have connections all through the city of Ottawa; another company might bring in an independent line at a small cost and take away a lot of the Bell subscribers if they could get connection free of charge. In the opinion of the sub-committee there might be a question of compensation in some cases, and for that reason the words were left in by the Senate. In any case, that is the way the Bill came from the Senate, and the Committee thought it wise to leave it as it was.

I was not on the Committee which dealt with this matter, and I am not as familiar with what took place as members of the Committee are. But I have a recollection of the debate that took place on this section a year ago, when the words "without compensation," were struck out of the Bill. These words, which were inserted by the Senate in the Bill this year, are evidently designed to enable the Bell Telephone Company to penalize any company that dares to compete with them. For many years the Bell Telephone Company, to which the people granted a very valuable franchise, neglected to extend its lines into rural districts; consequently, over six hundred telephone companies have been established in various parts of the country. I am familiar with the operation of the Inger-soll Telephone Company, which has been mentioned to-night. I believe it was singled out by the Bell Telephone Company as a company that dared enter into competition with the great Bell Company, in the town of Ingersoll; therefore a clause must be put in this Act to exact compensation from them.
What is meant by "compensation" in this case?

The Bell Telephone Company levies a tax of $300 a year upon outside companies for the privilege of connecting with the Bell lines. Besides, for every long distance call originating on the Ingersoll or on any other local line, ten cents additional has to be paid, of which the Bell Company takes seven cents and the local company three cents. Ten thousand calls must originate with the Ingersoll Company hefore they can get a cent of revenue out of this part of the service, because they have to pay $300 for the privilege of connecting with the Bell Telephone Company's line. As a matter of fact, these outside companies are of great service to the Bell Telephone Company; they enable it to reach the people in the rural districts. The number of longdistance calls originating on the Ingersoll line last year was 7,284; and 11,947 calls which originated on the Bell lines went over the Ingersoll lines. It seems to me that this charge of seven cents a call is ample compensation to the Bell Company. In justice to the local companies, an equal division should be made of that ten cents; the local company should get five cents and the Bell company five cents. That would be only fair, because the local -company is of as much service to the Bell company as

the Bell company is to the local company. For the life of me I cannot see why this provision should he in the Act. . In a case which came before the Railway Board some years ago and was submitted to the courts, one of the judges decided that as Parliament had not defined the matter clearly, but had put these words in the Act, they must have intended that compensation should he paid in some instances. Those instances only occur where a company is in competition with the Bell company. If you are going to encourage monopoly, if you are going to strangle initiative and enterprise on the part of weaker or smaller companies, then, I say, leave these words in. But if you are going to see that justice is done to all, regardless of whether they are weak or strong, these words should be struck out of the Bill.

I was a member of the special committee that dealt with this Bill, and listened to most of the discussion. I voted against the section as it now stands in the Bill, so that I feel free to vote for the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Wallace). The objection I have to mentioning compensation is that by doing so we imply that there are cases in which compensation ought to be given. I cannot make up my mind that there are any cases in which a tax of three, four or five hundred dollars should be imposed on a local company. The Bell Telephone company is looking for business; the greater the number of long distance messages brought to that company the more money they will make. It is an advantage to them to have the rural connection, and they get the lion's share of the ten cents extra that is paid by the sender of the message. This compensation is really used for the purpose of keeping down competition. The member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) told us that the Bell Telephone company did not insist upon exacting compensation in all cases; they asked for it only where there was competition. If, therefore, you give them the right to a compensation they will always ask for it for the purpose of keeping down competition. Why should Parliament assist the Bell Telephone company to keep down competition? The rates of the local lines, as well as those of the main line, are under the jurisdiction of the board, and if the local lines show a tendency to cut rates unduly the board will see that nothing unfair is done in that regard. There is no reason why compensation should be given when there is competition, but not when there is no competition. The objection is that the right to compensation

is used for an ulterior purpose, and is not in the public interest. The matter is not important so far as Nova Scotia is concerned, but I understand that eight or nine hundred lines in Ontario .which connect with the Bell Telephone company will be affected by our decision in this case. I intend to vote for my hon. friend's amendment.
, Mr. STEVENS:	This is a general Act
controlling railways, telephones, telegraphs, .etc., and it is administered very creditably by the Railway Commission. This clause .refers not only to any one particular telephone company, but to the telephone companies of Canada generally; it applies just as much to the British Columbia Telephone (Company as to the Bell Telephone Company in Ontario. Whenever a company or province, municipality or corporation desires to make a connection and cannot agree .wfth the telephone company with respect ,to obtaining such use, connection or com-.munication, such first mentioned company ,or province, municipality or corporation .may apply to the Board for relief. What ,1 want to impress upon the Committee is .this. This clause is not, as many hon. .members have intimated, some protection .for the Bell Telephone Company, but really ,a restriction on such Companies as the .Bell Telephone Company. It provides that other companies not having the advantage ,of these larger concerns may apply to the ,Board for the terms of their connections, .and the convenience of the public is undoubtedly considered by the Board as of .primary importance. The clause continues:
And the Board may order the company to provide for such use, connection or communication, upon such terms, including compensation if any.
The argument here is a question of fact. All those who are opposing the words now ,in the clause do so on the ground that there (should be no compensation, but we are not in a position to decide that no case .will arise anywhere in 'Canada where compensation may be desired. This works .both ways. It does not affect only the Bell .Telephone Company, although that company has been brought up as a sample .case, and if we strike out these words, we are preventing the Board of Railway Commissioners from giving compensation where cases are clearly made out. The point I wish to make plain is this. This court has been set up for the purpose of trying these cases on their merits; this Committee and the special committee cannot possibly expect to decide these cases on their merits,

and, therefore, we should give the Board the widest possible powers. I consider that those local companies, quoted so frequently here, are safe in the hands of the Board. I think we must all admit that. If the Railway Commission is not competent to administer this Act, then our first duty would be to make that court a competent court, but I submit that that court has, by its record, proved beyond all question that the public interest and the interests of various companies are quite safe in its charge. I feel it would be a serious mistake to restrict the powers of that Board to administer this clause or other clauses of a similar character in the Bill.

I quite agree with the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair). This is not a matter of want of confidence in the Railway Board at all; it is a matter for the Committee to decide. While I am not familiar with the telephone company of British Columbia, I am fairly familiar with the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, and if this Committee does not wish to say that the Bell Telephone Company, which is the great telephone company of this country, has a right to a monopoly and the right to make any other private or municipal company which wishes to use its long distance lines, pay the regular rate and to charge those people an extra ten cents, why should we not strike out those words?

As I understand the hon. member, he wants the clause framed so that the Bell Telephone Company cannot charge that ten cent rate for a local connection, but the striking out of the words "including compensation if any" would not do what he wants, because the clause still reads that the Board has power to order the connection on whatever terms it may deem just and fair.

The private companies would be perfectly satisfied if those words were struck out because, apparently, there has been in the past some decision on those very words. But apart from that altogether, I cannot bring myself to the conclusion that the Bell Telephone Company has a right to charge any other company an extra ten cents unless we of this Committee say: Yes, because you have a monopoly now, we shall let you keep it, and we shall permit you to penalize the other private or municipal companies, some two or three hundred in number throughout Canada.

This is not a question which affects only Ontario. As the bon.
member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has said, it affects any telephone company. Why is the Bell Telephone Company brought into this argument? Simply to becloud the issue and to endeavour to arouse sympathy. We are legislating for the whole of Canada. The Bell Telephone Company are not operating in Manitoba, and I do not know if they are operating in British Columbia. Supposing the British Columbia Telephone Company have some connection to make with any private telephone company, why should they be deprived of getting compensation before the Railway Board because there is a grievance in one or two provinces against one particular telephone company?
In one province.

I do not think that is fair. As the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has stated, we must either accept the Board of Railway Commissioners as a fair tribunal or not trust them. We may trust them to give justice, and what this Parliament seeks to do is to enact legislation that will give justice. If we do not trust them what is the use of having a Board of Railway Commissioners and of submitting to that board all differences which may arise under the Railway Act.
If we strike out those words, we curtail the powers of the board; we give notice to that court: We are willing that you should go a certain distance, but we do not trust you to go past that distance. I do not believe in limiting the jurisdiction of any court to serve a specific purpose, when in this Bill we are legislating, for the whole of Canada and for every citizen in Canada. The deeds of the board in the past are Such as to justify the confidence I have in them, and I am willing to trust them to remedy wrongs which may be done to any individual or company. We do not want to becloud the issue the same as was done as regards another Bill when it was made to appear that because certain members did|not agree to a clause in the Bill, they, were against public ownership of railways. That, was not the question, and that is not the question here. There is a tribunal to settle all these differences, and I think we can safely leave this matter to the board.

It is not simply a matter of the Bell Telephone company, but concerns every long-distance telephone company. The question for this committee to decide is whether the privately-owned and *the municipally-owned telephone companies [DOT]shall be compelled to pay the Bell Telephone Company, in addition to the regular rate, ten cents a message for long distance. I have confidence in the Board of Railway Commissioners, but is this committee going 'to say that every privately-owned and municipally-owned telephone company must 'apply to the Railway Board if it does not wish to pay that extra ten cents?

I have much pleasure in supporting the amendment moved by the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace). The people have found it necessary to build rural telephones for themselves because large corporations like the Bell Telephone have refused to do so. They had to invest money in these telephone companies, many of which I know have never paid one cent of interest. Then they have to pay for an expensive connection in order to get a long distance message over the 'phone. I claim that that is an injustice to the public. The telephone may be called a public utility, and its ex-

tension into the rural districts is going to be one of the great factors in keeping people on the land. We should encourage these small telephone companies instead of holding a club over them in the shape of a clause like this. I think it will be in the public interest to eliminate this clause altogether. Very few of these small companies pay more than operating expenses, while the Bell Telephone is one of the richest corporations in Canada to-day. The daily papers show that they are paying dividends of about 8 per cent, and now they are increasing their share issue and allot-ing them in the proportion of one to every four held, and a shareholder of the company will be able to get them for about 12 per cent less than the market value. I do not think this corporation needs any encouragement from this Parliament. I think we should pass legislation to protect the people, and especially the rural people, so that they will stay on the farm and produce, as they must produce if we are to pay off our national debt.
There are a good many companies that receive half on every call. I belong to two such companies myself.

There is a point that seems to have been overlooked in connection with the word " compensation." I believe there is a decision of the court in which it is held that when Parliament inserted the word " compensation " it was a reasonable presumption that the board must grant compensation whether they deemed it to he just or not. We can accept the judgments of the Railway Commission as being just, and our confidence in the commission would be best expressed if we omitted the word " compensation," for we would thereby leave the whole question to them. The clause without the word "compensation " will read:
the Board may order the company to provide for such use, connection or communication, upon such terms, including compensation-
If any.

Yes. The word was struck out by this Parliament in 1917 and reinserted by the Senate this year. The Senate reinserted the words " including compensation " and added " if any " afterwards. I am not a lawyer and do not presume to argue this question from the legal standpoint, but I think the majority of lawyers will agree with me that if we put in the words " including compensation if
any " there is a reasonable presumption that we anticipate that there will be compensation, and that we are directing the Board of Railway Commissioners to find compensation. Without these words we leave the whole matter to them, the same as we would any question of rates for the carriage of freight or passengers, or any other matter that rests with them.

I am in an awkward
position in regard to the amendment. I can support the striking out of the words "including compensation if any " but not the rest of the amendment. I think the board should have an entirely free hand as regards rates. I understand that the Supreme Court of Ontario decided that they felt themselves bound by some meaning attaching to the word " compensation." I am in favour of leaving these words out but I would not support the rest of the amendment.

That decision of the
court, I believe, was in connection with the original Railway Act, which read: "Upon such terms as to compensation as the board deems just and expedient." In that case it was decided that there should be compensation according to that interpretation. The words "if any" have been added so that it is plain the board will have power to decide whether there shall be any compensation or not. If these words were struck out the Board of Railway Commissioners would not have power to allow compensation even if it were considered that compensation should be allowed. The very fact of Parliamenthaving struck out the words would be interpreted as an intention on the part of Parliament that there should be no compensation, and the board would have no jurisdiction as regards compensation. If the rest of the clause is left in, they will, of course, have the right to arrange as regards rates and tolls.

I think the board will have every power they can possibly require, even after you have omitted these words on line 29. If they cannot give compensation they can increase the rates and even things up in that way. They need not call it compensation. We are giving them absolute power to deal with every phase of argument that can he presented by 'both sides. I have never had the pleasure of appearing before the hoard, who, I understand, are a very democratic court and will hear everything properly presented to them, and will make a decision covering the whole ground. It

is open to parties who go before them to argue as strongly as they can from both sides, and the board will reach its conclusions on the merits of the full facts. It is unnecessary to suggest to them that they have to consider the question of compensation. If it is decided to leave them a free hand without any encumbrance, in view of the decision of the Supreme 'Court of Ontario, I am in favour of striking these words out and will vote accordingly; but if the hon. member insists upon the rest of his amendment, I cannot vote for it.

The words "including compensation" are entirely superfluous. Their elimination would not detract from the powers of the board one iota. The matter would be fully covered if the section read:
The Board may order the company to provide for such use, connection or communication upon such terms as the Board deems just and expedient.
The word " compensation " is unnecessary, misleading and suggestive, and the board would have full power without them. The words " including compensation if any " are objected to by those who have experienced the effect of this clause. I have had communications from rural telephone companies in my riding and it is felt that these words should be eliminated.

I would move that the words " including compensation if any " on line 29 toe struck out.
